history.q: In which year did William of Normandy win the Battle of Hastings?
history.fact: The Bayeux Tapestry, nearly 70 metres long, tells the story of the Norman Conquest in embroidered scenes, right down to King Harold's death.

history.q: Which English king agreed to Magna Carta in 1215?
history.fact: Four original copies of the 1215 Magna Carta survive: two at the British Library, one at Lincoln Cathedral and one at Salisbury Cathedral.

history.q: Which Tudor monarch married six times?
history.fact: Schoolchildren remember the fates of his wives with the rhyme: "Divorced, beheaded, died; divorced, beheaded, survived."

history.q: In which year did the Great Fire of London destroy much of the medieval city?
history.fact: The fire began in a bakery on Pudding Lane and burned for about four days, destroying roughly 13,200 houses and 87 parish churches.

history.q: Which monarch was on the English throne when the Spanish Armada sailed in 1588?
history.fact: At Tilbury, Elizabeth told her troops: "I know I have the body of a weak and feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king."

history.q: In which year did the Acts of Union join England and Scotland into the Kingdom of Great Britain?
history.fact: The crowns had already been shared since 1603, when James VI of Scotland also became James I of England, over a century before the parliaments merged.

history.q: Which Roman emperor ordered a great defensive wall across northern Britain, begun around AD 122?
history.fact: Hadrian's Wall stretched about 73 miles (117 km) from the River Tyne to the Solway Firth, with small forts called milecastles along its length.

history.q: The Wars of the Roses were fought between the House of Lancaster and which other royal house?
history.fact: The wars ended in effect at Bosworth in 1485. The body of Richard III, the last English king to die in battle, was found under a Leicester car park in 2012.

history.q: Who was proclaimed queen in July 1553 but reigned for only about nine days?
history.fact: Lady Jane Grey was deposed by Mary I and executed at the Tower of London in February 1554, when she was only about 16 or 17 years old.

history.q: Which king was executed outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall in 1649?
history.fact: After his execution England was a republic for 11 years, until the monarchy was restored under his son Charles II in 1660.

history.q: Which queen reigned over Britain from 1837 to 1901?
history.fact: Victoria reigned for 63 years, the longest of any British monarch until Elizabeth II overtook her record in 2015.

history.q: Which British admiral was killed at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805?
history.fact: Nelson's body was brought home preserved in a cask of brandy. His statue has stood on top of Nelson's Column in Trafalgar Square since 1843.

history.q: What name is given to the failed 1605 conspiracy to blow up the Houses of Parliament?
history.fact: Guy Fawkes was caught guarding the barrels of gunpowder under the House of Lords. Britain still marks the night with bonfires and fireworks every 5 November.

history.q: Which 9th-century king of Wessex, who fought off Viking invaders, is known as "the Great"?
history.fact: Legend says that while hiding from the Vikings in the Somerset marshes, Alfred was scolded by a peasant woman for letting her cakes burn.

history.q: Which famous ocean liner, built in Belfast, sank on her maiden voyage in 1912?
history.fact: Titanic was built at the Harland and Wolff shipyard. The Titanic Belfast museum opened beside the old slipways in 2012, a century after she sank.

history.q: Which queen of the Iceni led a revolt against Roman rule in Britain around AD 60?
history.fact: Boudica's forces burned Camulodunum (Colchester), Londinium (London) and Verulamium (St Albans) before the Romans finally defeated them.

history.q: In which year was the Battle of Britain fought in the skies over southern England?
history.fact: Churchill praised the RAF pilots with the words: "Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few."

history.q: Which pandemic reached England in 1348 and killed a huge share of the population?
history.fact: Historians estimate the Black Death killed between a third and a half of England's people. The labour shortage it caused helped spark the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

history.q: Who led the Scottish army that defeated Edward II at the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314?
history.fact: In 1320 Scottish nobles sent the Declaration of Arbroath to the Pope, asking him to recognise Scotland's independence under Robert the Bruce.

history.q: Which Anglo-Saxon ship burial, uncovered in Suffolk in 1939, is famous for its ornate warrior's helmet?
history.fact: Landowner Edith Pretty donated the Sutton Hoo treasures to the British Museum. The story of the excavation inspired the 2021 film "The Dig".

history.q: Which 1746 battle near Inverness is known as the last pitched battle fought on British soil?
history.fact: Culloden ended the Jacobite rising of Bonnie Prince Charlie. He escaped to France, famously helped by Flora MacDonald, who disguised him as her maid.

history.q: In which year did the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland come into being?
history.fact: When Ireland joined the union on 1 January 1801, the red saltire of St Patrick was added to the flag, creating the Union Flag we know today.

history.q: Who led the Peasants' Revolt of 1381?
history.fact: Tyler was killed at Smithfield in London during a meeting with King Richard II, who was then only 14 years old.

history.q: Under which Roman emperor did the conquest of Britain begin in AD 43?
history.fact: According to the historian Cassius Dio, Claudius spent only about 16 days in Britain, entering Camulodunum (Colchester) with war elephants.

history.q: Which couple took the throne together after the Glorious Revolution of 1688?
choices: Charles II and Catherine of Braganza
James II and Mary of Modena
history.fact: William and Mary reigned as joint sovereigns, unique in British history. After Mary died in 1694, William ruled alone until 1702.

technology.q: Which naturalist set out the theory of evolution by natural selection in "On the Origin of Species" (1859)?
technology.fact: Darwin's ideas were shaped by his five-year voyage on HMS Beagle (1831-1836), including his visit to the Galapagos Islands.

technology.q: Which English scientist formulated the laws of motion and universal gravitation?
technology.fact: Newton published his Principia in 1687. Later in life he ran the Royal Mint, where he hunted down counterfeiters.

technology.q: Which British computer scientist invented the World Wide Web in 1989?
technology.fact: Berners-Lee wrote his proposal while working at CERN near Geneva, and the web's technology was released for anyone to use, royalty-free.

technology.q: Which Scottish scientist discovered penicillin in 1928?
technology.fact: Fleming noticed mould killing bacteria on a culture plate. He shared the 1945 Nobel Prize with Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, who turned it into a usable drug.

technology.q: Which Scottish inventor gave the first public demonstration of television in London in 1926?
technology.fact: Baird showed his moving television pictures to members of the Royal Institution in an attic workshop on Frith Street in Soho in January 1926.

technology.q: Which Scottish engineer's improved steam engine, with a separate condenser, helped power the Industrial Revolution?
technology.fact: The watt, the standard unit of power printed on every light bulb, is named in his honour.

technology.q: At which wartime codebreaking centre did Alan Turing help crack the German Enigma code?
technology.fact: Turing's portrait has appeared on the Bank of England's £50 note since 2021, alongside a quote about the future of computing.

technology.q: Dolly, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell (born in Scotland in 1996), was what kind of animal?
technology.fact: Dolly was created at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh and was named after singer Dolly Parton, because she was cloned from a mammary gland cell.

technology.q: Ada Lovelace's famous 1843 notes described which machine designed by Charles Babbage?
technology.fact: Her notes include a method for calculating Bernoulli numbers, often called the first published computer program.

technology.q: Which English scientist discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831?
technology.fact: Faraday had little formal schooling. He started as a bookbinder's apprentice before becoming Humphry Davy's assistant at the Royal Institution.

technology.q: Which Scottish-born inventor was granted the first US patent for the telephone in 1876?
technology.fact: Bell was born in Edinburgh in 1847. His family emigrated to Canada in 1870, and he later taught deaf students in Boston.

technology.q: Which Victorian engineer built the Great Western Railway and the steamship SS Great Britain?
technology.fact: In a 2002 BBC poll of the 100 Greatest Britons, Brunel came second, behind only Winston Churchill.

technology.q: Which British physicist wrote the bestselling book "A Brief History of Time" (1988)?
technology.fact: Hawking held Cambridge's Lucasian Professorship of Mathematics for 30 years, the same chair once held by Isaac Newton.

technology.q: Which famous RAF fighter plane of the Battle of Britain was designed by R. J. Mitchell?
technology.fact: Mitchell died of cancer in 1937, aged 42, so he never saw his Spitfire go into battle.

technology.q: Which time standard is named after a district of London that is home to the Royal Observatory?
technology.fact: At a conference in Washington in 1884, delegates chose the meridian through Greenwich as the world's Prime Meridian, longitude 0°.

technology.q: Which British scientist, with American James Watson, proposed the double-helix structure of DNA in 1953?
technology.fact: A plaque at the Eagle pub in Cambridge marks where, by Watson's account, Crick announced they had found "the secret of life".

technology.q: Which English engineer patented a design for the turbojet engine in 1930?
technology.fact: In Germany, Hans von Ohain developed a jet engine independently, and a German jet made the first jet-powered flight in 1939.

technology.q: Which railway, opened in 1825, was the world's first public railway to use steam locomotives?
technology.fact: George Stephenson's Locomotion No. 1 hauled the opening train on 27 September 1825, and the line's bicentenary was celebrated in 2025.

technology.q: Which Scottish physicist's equations showed that light is an electromagnetic wave?
technology.fact: Maxwell's method also produced the first lasting colour photograph, an image of a tartan ribbon, shown in 1861.

technology.q: Which English doctor developed the first vaccine, against smallpox, in 1796?
technology.fact: Jenner used cowpox from a milkmaid to protect a boy named James Phipps. The word "vaccine" comes from the Latin "vacca", meaning cow.

technology.q: Which English physician described how the heart pumps blood around the body in 1628?
technology.fact: Harvey set out his discovery in the book "De Motu Cordis". He was physician to both James I and Charles I.

technology.q: Which London doctor traced an 1854 cholera outbreak to a water pump on Broad Street in Soho?
technology.fact: A replica of the handle-less pump stands today on Broadwick Street, close to a pub named in Snow's honour.

technology.q: Which surgeon pioneered antiseptic surgery using carbolic acid in the 1860s?
technology.fact: Lister's work saved countless lives from infection. The mouthwash Listerine, created in 1879, was named in his honour.

technology.q: Which British engineer invented the hovercraft in the 1950s?
technology.fact: The first full-size hovercraft, the SR.N1, crossed the English Channel in July 1959, exactly 50 years after Louis Blériot first flew across it.

technology.q: Which Victorian engineer built London's great sewer network after the "Great Stink" of 1858?
technology.fact: Bazalgette hid his main sewers inside new Thames embankments. The Victoria Embankment also carries a London Underground line.

art.q: Who wrote the play "Romeo and Juliet"?
art.fact: Shakespeare's Globe on London's South Bank is a reconstruction of his playhouse. It opened in 1997, close to the site of the original 1599 theatre.

art.q: Which Liverpool band released the 1969 album "Abbey Road"?
art.fact: The zebra crossing on the album cover, outside Abbey Road Studios in London, was given Grade II listed status in 2010.

art.q: Who wrote the 1813 novel "Pride and Prejudice"?
art.fact: Jane Austen's portrait has appeared on the Bank of England £10 note since 2017, the 200th anniversary of her death.

art.q: Which author created the detective Sherlock Holmes?
art.fact: Conan Doyle trained as a doctor in Edinburgh. His teacher Dr Joseph Bell, famous for his sharp powers of observation, inspired Holmes.

art.q: Which painter created "The Fighting Temeraire" (1839)?
art.fact: Turner is known as the "painter of light". Since 2020 his self-portrait and "The Fighting Temeraire" have appeared on the Bank of England £20 note.

art.q: Which architect designed St Paul's Cathedral in London after the Great Fire?
art.fact: Wren is buried in the cathedral. His epitaph reads: "Reader, if you seek his monument, look around you."

art.q: Which novel did Mary Shelley publish in 1818?
choices: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
art.fact: Mary Shelley started the story at 18, during a ghost-story contest with Lord Byron near Lake Geneva in the stormy summer of 1816.

art.q: Which London-born film director was known as the "Master of Suspense"?
art.fact: Hitchcock made brief cameo appearances in many of his own films, and fans still enjoy spotting him in the background.

art.q: Which English composer wrote the "Pomp and Circumstance" marches, including the tune of "Land of Hope and Glory"?
art.fact: Elgar's "Enigma Variations" (1899) are dedicated "to my friends pictured within", and each variation is a musical portrait of someone he knew.

art.q: Which sculptor created the "Angel of the North" near Gateshead?
art.fact: Completed in 1998, the steel angel stands 20 metres tall. Its 54-metre wings are angled slightly forward to create a sense of embrace.

art.q: Who wrote the 1843 novella "A Christmas Carol"?
art.fact: Dickens wrote "A Christmas Carol" in about six weeks, and the first 6,000 copies sold out by Christmas Eve 1843.

art.q: Which British author created the Harry Potter books?
art.fact: Rowling has said the idea for Harry Potter came to her in 1990, on a delayed train from Manchester to London King's Cross.

art.q: Which London rock band released "Bohemian Rhapsody" in 1975?
art.fact: Although it is about six minutes long and has no chorus, "Bohemian Rhapsody" spent nine weeks at number one in the UK in 1975-76.

art.q: Which fictional spy, codenamed 007, was created by author Ian Fleming?
art.fact: Fleming borrowed the name from an American ornithologist, James Bond, author of the book "Birds of the West Indies".

art.q: Who wrote "Alice's Adventures in Wonderland" (1865)?
art.fact: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Dodgson, an Oxford mathematics lecturer who first told the story to young Alice Liddell.

art.q: Which Brontë sister wrote "Jane Eyre" (1847)?
art.fact: Charlotte first published "Jane Eyre" under the male pen name Currer Bell. Her sisters wrote as Ellis and Acton Bell.

art.q: Which artist painted "The Hay Wain" (1821)?
art.fact: The painting shows a scene near Flatford Mill on the River Stour in Suffolk. Willy Lott's Cottage, seen on the left, still stands.

art.q: Who wrote the dystopian novel "Nineteen Eighty-Four" (1949)?
art.fact: George Orwell was the pen name of Eric Arthur Blair. He finished the novel in a remote farmhouse on the Scottish island of Jura.

art.q: Which German-born composer wrote the oratorio "Messiah", first performed in 1742?
art.fact: Handel became a British subject in 1727 and spent most of his career in London. He is buried in Westminster Abbey.

art.q: Which anonymous street artist's "Girl with Balloon" shredded itself moments after being sold at auction in 2018?
art.fact: The half-shredded work was renamed "Love is in the Bin". When it was resold in 2021, it fetched about £18.6 million.

art.q: Which poet wrote "The Rime of the Ancient Mariner"?
art.fact: The poem first appeared in "Lyrical Ballads" (1798), a joint collection with Wordsworth that helped launch English Romanticism.

art.q: Which Pre-Raphaelite artist painted "Ophelia" (1851-52)?
art.fact: The model, Elizabeth Siddal, posed in a bath of water warmed by lamps. When they went out, she reportedly fell seriously ill.

art.q: Which English composer wrote the orchestral suite "The Planets"?
art.fact: Holst wrote "The Planets" in 1914-1916, so it has no movement for Pluto, which was not discovered until 1930.

art.q: Which architect remodelled the Royal Pavilion in Brighton in an Indian-inspired style for the Prince Regent?
art.fact: Nash also laid out Regent Street and the terraces around Regent's Park, both named after his patron, the future George IV.

art.q: Which English playwright wrote "Look Back in Anger" (1956)?
art.fact: After its premiere at London's Royal Court Theatre, critics began calling a new generation of writers the "angry young men".

politics.q: What is the address of the UK Prime Minister's official London residence and office?
politics.fact: Downing Street is named after Sir George Downing, a 17th-century diplomat and property developer who built the street's houses.

politics.q: What is the upper chamber of the UK Parliament called?
politics.fact: Most members of the House of Lords are appointed rather than elected. They include 26 Church of England bishops, known as the Lords Spiritual.

politics.q: Who was the first woman to serve as UK Prime Minister?
politics.fact: Thatcher served from 1979 to 1990, the longest continuous term of any British Prime Minister in the 20th century.

politics.q: Who became Prime Minister in May 1940 and led Britain through most of the Second World War?
politics.fact: Churchill was also a prolific writer. He won the 1953 Nobel Prize in Literature, in part for his historical writing and his speeches.

politics.q: Who is generally regarded as Britain's first Prime Minister?
politics.fact: Walpole led the government from 1721 to 1742. At about 21 years, that is still the longest time anyone has served as Prime Minister.

politics.q: In which year did the UK hold its referendum on leaving the European Union?
politics.fact: Leave won by 51.9% to 48.1%, on a turnout of about 72%, which was the highest turnout at any UK-wide vote since 1992.

politics.q: Which court became the UK's highest court of appeal in 2009, replacing the House of Lords in that role?
politics.fact: The Supreme Court sits in the Middlesex Guildhall on Parliament Square, directly across from the Houses of Parliament.

politics.q: In which year did the devolved Scottish Parliament first meet?
politics.fact: For its first five years it met in the Church of Scotland's Assembly Hall. Its own building at Holyrood in Edinburgh opened in 2004.

politics.q: Which 1689 Act, passed after the Glorious Revolution, limited the powers of the monarch?
politics.fact: The Bill of Rights also protects free speech in Parliament: what MPs say in debates cannot be challenged in any court, a rule still in force today.

politics.q: In which year did women in the UK gain the right to vote on equal terms with men?
politics.fact: In 1918 only some women over 30 could vote. The Equal Franchise Act of 1928 lowered the voting age for women to 21, the same as for men.

politics.q: In which chamber of the UK Parliament do elected MPs sit?
politics.fact: The Commons benches are green. Red lines on the floor, said to be two sword-lengths apart, mark where members may not cross during debates.

politics.q: Which party did Tony Blair lead to a landslide general election victory in 1997?
politics.fact: Labour won 418 seats in 1997, giving it a majority of 179, the largest in the party's history.

politics.q: Which government minister presents the annual Budget to Parliament?
politics.fact: By tradition, the Chancellor poses outside 11 Downing Street holding up a red despatch box before delivering the Budget speech.

politics.q: Which Prime Minister called the 2016 EU referendum and resigned after the Leave vote?
politics.fact: Cameron later returned to government as Foreign Secretary in 2023, after being made a member of the House of Lords as Lord Cameron.

politics.q: What is the title of the person who chairs debates in the House of Commons?
politics.fact: By tradition, a newly elected Speaker is dragged to the chair by other MPs, a reminder of days when the job could be dangerous.

politics.q: What is the speech called in which the monarch sets out the government's plans at the State Opening of Parliament?
politics.fact: Before the speech, Black Rod summons MPs to the Lords, but first has the Commons door slammed in their face, a symbol of the Commons' independence.

politics.q: Which Prime Minister's government created the National Health Service in 1948?
politics.fact: The NHS was launched on 5 July 1948 by Health Minister Aneurin Bevan, offering care that was free at the point of use.

politics.q: Which 1998 peace deal set up a power-sharing government in Northern Ireland?
politics.fact: The agreement was approved by voters in referendums held on the same day, 22 May 1998, in both Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland.

politics.q: How many MPs sit in the House of Commons?
politics.fact: The Commons chamber has seats for only about 427 MPs, so members often stand or sit on the steps during busy debates.

politics.q: Which Victorian politician served as Prime Minister four separate times?
politics.fact: Gladstone was still Prime Minister at the age of 84 when he left office in 1894, making him the oldest person ever to hold the job.

politics.q: Which 1832 Act reformed the voting system and abolished many "rotten boroughs"?
politics.fact: Old Sarum in Wiltshire, an almost empty hilltop, elected two MPs until the Act abolished it.

politics.q: Which 1911 Act removed the House of Lords' power to veto most bills?
politics.fact: The same Act cut the maximum time between general elections from seven years to five.

politics.q: Who became Britain's first Labour Prime Minister in 1924?
politics.fact: MacDonald's first government lasted less than a year. He returned as Prime Minister from 1929 to 1935.

politics.q: Which British Prime Minister was assassinated in 1812?
politics.fact: Perceval was shot in the lobby of the House of Commons by John Bellingham. He is the only British Prime Minister to have been assassinated.

politics.q: Who became the first woman Speaker of the House of Commons in 1992?
politics.fact: Before entering politics, Betty Boothroyd danced professionally as one of the Tiller Girls.

current-affairs.q: Who became UK Prime Minister in July 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Labour won 411 seats at the general election on 4 July 2024, ending 14 years of Conservative-led government.

current-affairs.q: In which year did Queen Elizabeth II die?
current-affairs.fact: She died at Balmoral on 8 September 2022 after reigning for 70 years, longer than any other British monarch.

current-affairs.q: In which year was King Charles III crowned at Westminster Abbey?
current-affairs.fact: The coronation took place on 6 May 2023. Westminster Abbey has hosted English and British coronations since 1066.

current-affairs.q: Who became the shortest-serving UK Prime Minister in history, leaving office after about 49 days in October 2022?
current-affairs.fact: While she was in office, a tabloid livestreamed a lettuce to see whether it would last longer than her premiership. The lettuce won.

current-affairs.q: Which new railway line through central London opened in May 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Built by the Crossrail project, the line runs under central London and links Reading and Heathrow in the west with Shenfield and Abbey Wood in the east.

current-affairs.q: Which major tournament did England's women's football team, the Lionesses, win in 2022?
current-affairs.fact: They beat Germany 2-1 after extra time at Wembley, giving England its first major senior football trophy since the men's World Cup in 1966.

current-affairs.q: Who became the UK's first British Asian Prime Minister in October 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Before becoming Prime Minister, Sunak was Chancellor of the Exchequer during the COVID-19 pandemic and launched the furlough scheme.

current-affairs.q: The post-Brexit transition period, when the UK still followed EU single-market rules, ended on 31 December of which year?
current-affairs.fact: The UK formally left the EU on 31 January 2020, but trade carried on under EU rules until the transition period ended at the close of that year.

current-affairs.q: Who was elected leader of the Conservative Party in November 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Badenoch became the first Black woman to lead a major UK political party, taking over from Rishi Sunak after the 2024 election defeat.

current-affairs.q: Which English city hosted the 2022 Commonwealth Games?
current-affairs.fact: Women's T20 cricket made its Commonwealth Games debut at Birmingham 2022. Cricket had last featured, for men only, in 1998.

current-affairs.q: Which party leader won the UK general election of December 2019?
current-affairs.fact: Campaigning on the slogan "Get Brexit Done", Johnson's Conservatives won an 80-seat majority.

current-affairs.q: Which country beat England on penalties in the final of Euro 2020, played at Wembley in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Euro 2020 was postponed by a year because of the COVID-19 pandemic but kept its original name.

current-affairs.q: Which British teenager won the 2021 US Open women's singles title?
current-affairs.fact: Raducanu, aged 18, became the first qualifier ever to win a Grand Slam singles title, and she did it without dropping a set.

current-affairs.q: Which royal couple announced in January 2020 that they would step back as senior working royals?
current-affairs.fact: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex later settled in Montecito, California.

current-affairs.q: In December 2020 the UK became the first country to approve which company's COVID-19 vaccine, made with BioNTech?
current-affairs.fact: Margaret Keenan, aged 90, was the first person to receive the approved vaccine, at a hospital in Coventry on 8 December 2020.

current-affairs.q: Oxford University developed a COVID-19 vaccine in partnership with which company?
current-affairs.fact: AstraZeneca agreed to supply the Oxford vaccine on a not-for-profit basis during the pandemic.

current-affairs.q: Who succeeded Nicola Sturgeon as First Minister of Scotland in March 2023?
current-affairs.fact: Yousaf was the first Muslim to lead a devolved UK government. He resigned in 2024 and was succeeded by John Swinney.

current-affairs.q: Who became the UK's first female Chancellor of the Exchequer in July 2024?
current-affairs.fact: The office of Chancellor of the Exchequer dates back to the 13th century, making Reeves the first woman in the job in roughly 800 years.

current-affairs.q: Which party, led by Nigel Farage, won five seats at the July 2024 general election?
current-affairs.fact: Farage won the Essex seat of Clacton, entering the House of Commons on his eighth attempt.

current-affairs.q: Who became Northern Ireland's first nationalist First Minister in February 2024?
current-affairs.fact: The First Minister and deputy First Minister have equal powers. Emma Little-Pengelly of the DUP became deputy First Minister alongside O'Neill.

current-affairs.q: In July 2023 the UK signed up to join which Asia-Pacific trade agreement?
current-affairs.fact: The UK became the first new member of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, and its first European one, in December 2024.

current-affairs.q: Who was elected Speaker of the House of Commons in November 2019, succeeding John Bercow?
current-affairs.fact: Hoyle is known for naming his pets after politicians, including a tortoise called Maggie and a parrot called Boris.

current-affairs.q: Who became the first woman to serve as First Minister of Wales, in August 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Morgan succeeded Vaughan Gething, who resigned after only about four months as First Minister.

current-affairs.q: At which historic site did the UK host the first global AI Safety Summit in November 2023?
current-affairs.fact: The summit produced the Bletchley Declaration on AI risks, signed by 28 countries and the European Union.

current-affairs.q: Which club did Manchester City beat in the 2023 Champions League final to complete a treble?
current-affairs.fact: Rodri scored the only goal in Istanbul. City became the second English men's club to win the treble, after Manchester United in 1999.

general.q: What is the capital of Scotland?
general.fact: Every August Edinburgh hosts the Festival Fringe, often called the world's largest arts festival, with thousands of shows across the city.

general.q: What is the highest mountain in the United Kingdom?
general.fact: Ben Nevis rises 1,345 metres above Fort William. A weather observatory once operated on its summit, from 1883 to 1904.

general.q: What is the nickname of the great bell in the clock tower at the Palace of Westminster?
general.fact: The clock tower was renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012 to mark Queen Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee.

general.q: Which Grand Slam tennis tournament is held in London every summer?
general.fact: First held in 1877, Wimbledon is the oldest tennis tournament in the world and the only Grand Slam still played on grass.

general.q: What is the longest river in the United Kingdom?
general.fact: The Severn runs about 220 miles (354 km) from the Welsh mountains of Plynlimon to the Bristol Channel, and is famous for its tidal bore.

general.q: Who is the patron saint of Wales?
general.fact: St David's Day is celebrated on 1 March, when many people in Wales wear a daffodil or a leek, both national emblems.

general.q: In which English county is Stonehenge?
general.fact: Stonehenge's smaller bluestones were brought from the Preseli Hills in Wales, about 150 miles away, thousands of years ago.

general.q: Which sport takes its name from the English school where it is said to have begun?
general.fact: Legend says that in 1823 a pupil named William Webb Ellis picked up the ball and ran with it. The Rugby World Cup trophy is named after him.

general.q: Which lake holds the largest volume of fresh water in the United Kingdom?
general.fact: Loch Ness is so deep that it holds more fresh water than all the lakes in England and Wales put together.

general.q: Which island group is the northernmost part of the United Kingdom?
general.fact: Shetland is closer to Norway than to London. Its Norse heritage lives on in Up Helly Aa, a winter fire festival where a Viking longship is burned.

general.q: What is the capital city of Wales?
general.fact: Cardiff only officially became the capital of Wales in 1955, making it one of the youngest capital cities in Europe.

general.q: Which London palace is the official residence of the British monarch?
general.fact: Buckingham Palace has 775 rooms. When the monarch is in residence, the Royal Standard flies from its flagpole instead of the Union Flag.

general.q: Which river flows through the heart of London?
general.fact: The Thames Barrier, in use since 1982, can close its giant steel gates to protect London from flooding by storm surges from the North Sea.

general.q: Which London stadium is home to the England national football team?
general.fact: The new Wembley, opened in 2007, is crowned by a 133-metre steel arch that can be seen from across London.

general.q: Which English city has the oldest university in the English-speaking world?
general.fact: There is evidence of teaching at Oxford as early as 1096. Cambridge University was founded in 1209 by scholars who left Oxford.

general.q: What is the national animal of Scotland?
general.fact: The royal coat of arms shows two supporters: a lion for England and a unicorn for Scotland.

general.q: Which Scottish town is known as the "Home of Golf"?
general.fact: St Andrews' Old Course has hosted The Open more often than any other venue, including the 150th Open in 2022.

general.q: What is the national flower of England?
general.fact: The Tudor rose combined the red rose of Lancaster with the white rose of York after Henry VII married Elizabeth of York.

general.q: Which Northern Irish landmark is made up of about 40,000 interlocking basalt columns?
general.fact: Legend says the giant Finn McCool built the causeway to cross the sea to Scotland. Geologists say the columns formed as lava cooled.

general.q: Which Scottish poet's birthday is celebrated with suppers every 25 January?
general.fact: Burns wrote down the words of "Auld Lang Syne", now sung around the world as the clock strikes midnight on New Year's Eve.

general.q: Which lake in Northern Ireland is the largest lake by area in the UK?
general.fact: Lough Neagh covers about 390 km² and touches five of Northern Ireland's six counties.

general.q: Which is the largest national park in the United Kingdom?
general.fact: The Cairngorms are home to Britain's only free-ranging herd of reindeer.

general.q: Which narrow stretch of water separates the island of Anglesey from mainland Wales?
general.fact: Thomas Telford's Menai Suspension Bridge, opened in 1826, was one of the first modern suspension bridges in the world.

general.q: Which long-distance footpath became Britain's first National Trail in 1965?
general.fact: The Pennine Way runs about 268 miles (431 km) from Edale in Derbyshire to Kirk Yetholm, just over the Scottish border.

general.q: Which Hebridean island is famous for peaty single-malt whiskies such as Laphroaig and Lagavulin?
general.fact: Islay is nicknamed the "Queen of the Hebrides". Its whiskies get their smoky taste from malted barley dried over peat fires.
